fields.category: Black currant cultivars for the Inland Northwest and Intermountain West

rows.name: Ben Alder
rows.comments: Produces high quality juice. Vigorous, late flowering, and somewhat resistant to spring frosts. High yielding under ideal conditions, but yields can be low

rows.name: Ben Connan
rows.comments: Deep black berries. Suitable for fresh use and processing. Not ideal for juice. Tolerates spring frosts. Can produce high yields. Compact bushes. Suitable for machine harvesting

rows.name: Ben Lomond
rows.comments: Blooms late and is frost resistant. Consistently high yields. Moderately vigorous. Recommended for commercial fresh and processing markets, U-pick, and home production. Machine harvestable

rows.name: Ben Sarek
rows.comments: Compact plant that is moderately resistant to white pine blister rust and powdery mildew. Very high yielding with very large berries. Used mainly for pick-your-own and home use, not commercial juice production

rows.name: Boskoop Giant
rows.comments: Long loose clusters. Berries near cluster tips often abort due to poor pollination. Vigorous. Plants labeled Boskoop Giant are not always true-to-name. Fragrant leaves and buds are reportedly suited for teas

rows.name: Champion
rows.comments: Mild-flavored berries with good quality but variable size and uneven ripening. Vigorous

rows.name: Consort
rows.comments: Resistant to blister rust but highly susceptible to powdery mildew. Poor fruit quality. If blister rust is a concern, Titania and Ben Sarek are better choices

rows.name: Crusader
rows.comments: Resistant to blister rust but highly susceptible to powdery mildew. Poor fruit quality. If blister rust is a concern, Titania and Ben Sarek are better choices

rows.name: Coronet
rows.comments: Resistant to blister rust but highly susceptible to powdery mildew. Poor fruit quality. If blister rust is a concern, Titania and Ben Sarek are better choices

rows.name: Crandall
rows.comments: Selection of North American golden currant used as an ornamental. Weak canes droop under crop loads, making trellises desirable. Ripe berries have a mild, pleasant flavor different from European black currants. Performs well in areas with hot summers

rows.name: Kerry
rows.comments: Canes are vigorous and productive

rows.name: Strata
rows.comments: Berries are sweet and suited for fresh use or processing. Canes are moderately vigorous. Yields can be low

rows.name: Swedish Black
rows.comments: Very sweet berries with excellent flavor. Canes are moderately vigorous and sprawling, making management somewhat difficult. Yields can be low

rows.name: Titania
rows.comments: Ripens uniformly. Mild-flavored, but bitter fruit flavor can occur. Highly self-fertile. Vigorous and high yielding. Suitable for commercial and home production. Immune to blister rust but susceptible to botryosphaeria cane dieback

rows.name: Topsy
rows.comments: Thick-skinned fruits ripen during mid-season. Canes are vigorous

fields.category: Red currant cultivars for the Inland Northwest and Intermountain West

rows.name: Cascade
rows.comments: Berries are high in sugar and have good flavor. Moderately vigorous

rows.name: Jonkheer van Tets
rows.comments: Berries are variable in size, of average quality, and can split in wet weather. Vigorous. Very popular in Europe

rows.name: Laxton's No. 1
rows.comments: Berries have good quality and are tightly bunched on the strigs. Very productive. Popular commercially in Europe

rows.name: Minnesota No. 71
rows.comments: Consistent fruit quality. Vigorous. Popular for commercial use in England. One of the best cultivars in North America

rows.name: Perfection
rows.comments: Good flavor but sunscalds easily. Long, easy-to-pick clusters. Vigorous canes are susceptible to breaking. Very cold hardy. For commercial production in colder areas

rows.name: Portal Ruby
rows.comments: Berries are tart. Canes are moderately vigorous

rows.name: Prince Albert
rows.comments: Berries hang well without overripening. Long, easy-to-pick stems. Moderately vigorous. Excellent late-season cultivar, particularly for U-pick

rows.name: Red Lake
rows.comments: Good flavor. Moderately vigorous. Clusters are long and easy to pick. Excellent for commercial and home production

rows.name: Rondom
rows.comments: Berries hang well without overripening. Long, easy-to-pick clusters. Vigorous. Popular commercially in Europe. Immune to blister rust

rows.name: Rosetta
rows.comments: Berries are tart. Long, easy-to-pick clusters. Moderately vigorous. Promising recent introduction

rows.name: Rovada
rows.comments: Late ripening. Long, easy-to-pick clusters. Moderately susceptible to fruit run off. Resistant to leaf spot. High yields. Popular commercially in Central Europe

rows.name: Stanza
rows.comments: Long, easy-to-pick stems. Suitable for fresh use and especially for juicing. Acidic flavor. Canes are moderately vigorous and reliably productive

rows.name: Stephens No. 9
rows.comments: Canes are vigorous. One of the most popular red currants in North America

rows.name: Tatran
rows.comments: Berries have good quality and are borne on exceptionally long clusters. High yields reported. Vigorous and cold hardy

rows.name: Victoria
rows.comments: Small firm berries hang well without overripening. Vigorous, productive, and very cold hardy. With mechanical harvesting, may be suitable for commercial processing markets

rows.name: Wilder
rows.comments: Berries are variable in size, have good quality, and hang well without overripening. Long, easy-to-pick clusters. Vigorous. Good commercial or home choice

fields.category: White currant cultivars for the Inland Northwest and Intermountain West

rows.name: Blanka
rows.comments: Late ripening, very productive, and very resistant to frosts. Persistent for a long season. New to North America. From Slovakia. Fruit run-off can be high

rows.name: Gloire des Sablons
rows.comments: Pinkish-white fruits with average flavor and quality. European heritage cultivar

rows.name: Primus
rows.comments: Berries have good flavor and are whiter than some other white currants. Yields can be high. New to North America. From Slovakia

rows.name: White Currant 1301
rows.comments: Medium-sized berries on moderately vigorous canes that are somewhat resistant to powdery mildew and resistant to blister rust. From Sweden

rows.name: White Dutch
rows.comments: Excellent quality berries ripen early and are darker than other white currants. Vigorous and very productive. Small uneven berry size is the main limitation. European heritage cultivar

rows.name: White Imperial
rows.comments: Moderately vigorous and productive. Excellent for commercial and home production. European heritage cultivar

rows.name: White Versailles
rows.comments: Berries have good quality and are borne on long clusters. Vigorous. European heritage cultivar

fields.category: American gooseberry cultivars for the Inland Northwest and Intermountain West

rows.name: Captivator
rows.comments: Greenish-red to red fruit. Good flavor. Moderately vigorous and less spiny than some cultivars. Excellent for commercial and home production

rows.name: Glenndale
rows.comments: Moderate quality dark red to purple berries. Can produce high yields. Canes are very thorny and vigorous. Tolerates bright sun and high temperatures

rows.name: Jahn's Prairie
rows.comments: Red-pink high quality dessert gooseberry. High yields. Thorny. Somewhat slow to mature. For home use and commercial testing. Resistant to blister rust, leaf spot, stem Botrytis, aphids, and sawflies

rows.name: Jeanne
rows.comments: Newly released dark red, late ripening, disease resistant dessert gooseberry

rows.name: Oregon
rows.comments: Also known as Oregon Champion. Tart white to pale green berries. Best suited to processing. Vigorous

rows.name: Pixwell
rows.comments: Pale green to pinkish-red berries hang below the canes, facilitating hand picking. Can become bitter when overripe. Vigorous. Very reliable. Best suited to processing

rows.name: Poorman
rows.comments: Red berries are sweet, aromatic, and begin ripening in midseason. Vigorous with fewer spines than some cultivars. One of the best gooseberries for North America

rows.name: Stanbridge
rows.comments: Yellowish-green fruits. Yields are moderate. Canes are erect, vigorous, and develop few or no spines

rows.name: Welcome
rows.comments: Red fruit. Canes are initially weak and spreading but become more vigorous and erect as the plant matures. Widely available in the United States

fields.category: European gooseberry cultivars for the Inland Northwest and Intermountain West

rows.name: Chautauqua
rows.comments: Green fruit with good flavor and quality. Canes are dense, spreading, and moderately erect. One of the most promising European gooseberries for North America

rows.name: Green Hansa
rows.comments: Green fruits are suitable for dessert use. Canes are below average in size and vigor

rows.name: Greenfinch
rows.comments: Mid-season ripening with green-yellow fruit

rows.name: Keepsake
rows.comments: Greenish-red berries are variable in size. Fruit quality is good, but size variability limits commercial value. Moderately vigorous

rows.name: Lepaa Red
rows.comments: Small red berries have good flavor. Plants are small, vigorous, and productive. Highly reliable. Best suited for processing, but fresh flavor may make it useful for farmers markets

rows.name: Malling Invicta
rows.comments: Early ripening, very high yielding, with large yellow fruits

rows.name: May Duke
rows.comments: Green to dull red berries when ripe and pleasantly flavored. Vigorous

rows.name: Speedwell
rows.comments: Red, sweet berries with fair quality. Canes are moderately vigorous

fields.category: Jostaberry cultivars for the Inland Northwest and Intermountain West

rows.name: Josta
rows.comments: Widely available in North America. Reported self-fertile, but North American growers have reported poor fruit set. Resistant to blister rust under field conditions

rows.name: Jostine
rows.comments: Imported into the United States but not yet widely available. At least partially self-sterile and should be planted with Jogranda for good fruit set

rows.name: Jogranda
rows.comments: Also known as Jostagranda and Jostaki. Imported into the United States but not yet widely available. At least partially self-sterile and should be planted with Jostine for good fruit set
